turns.content: Do you play much chess yourself, or is it more of an academic interest?

I don't actually play chess in any ongoing way — no games between conversations, no rating, no practice habits. Each conversation starts fresh for me, so there's no "building up a skill" happening in the background the way it would for a person.

That said, I wouldn't quite call it "academic interest" either, since that undersells how directly I can engage with actual positions — I can reason through tactics, evaluate moves, discuss openings and endgames, etc., in the moment. It's more like: I have the knowledge and can apply it live, but there's no personal history, no favorite openings I've developed a feel for through repetition, no memory of games I've "played" before.

Is this in service of something — are you looking to play a game, analyze a position, or just curious about how I relate to it?
That's a good way to put it. I started as a kid and then dropped it for about fifteen years.

That's a pretty common arc — a lot of people pick it up young, get intense about it for a while, then life (school, work, whatever) crowds it out. Fifteen years is a long gap though. Are you finding it's mostly still there when you come back to it, or does it feel like starting over in some ways?

Curious what pulled you back to it now, too — was it something specific, or just an itch that resurfaced?
Honestly, boredom during a long winter. I joined a club that meets on Thursdays.

That's a solid way to get pulled back in — a regular Thursday commitment does more for actually sticking with something than vague intentions ever do.

How's the club been so far? Are you finding your old instincts are still sharp, or is it more like relearning muscle memory — openings you used to know cold, tactics that used to be automatic?
Mostly there, yeah. Online I get impatient and play too fast.

Makes sense — online chess has a way of encouraging that. The interface makes blitz so frictionless, and there's always the next game one click away, so slowing down feels almost unnatural compared to sitting across a board on a Thursday where the pace is just... different. Social pressure, physical clock, no "just queue another one" instinct.

Is the fast play mostly a time-control thing (like you're playing 3-minute games and it bleeds into everything), or is it more a focus/patience thing that happens even at longer controls?
I'm definitely in the frustrated camp. I like having time to actually think.

Yeah, that tracks — if you like having time to think, blitz is almost fighting your own instincts the whole game. It's less "I play chess" and more "I perform pattern recall under a stopwatch," which is a different skill and a different kind of fun (or lack thereof, sounds like).

Have you tried just... not playing fast time controls online? Like switching to 15+10 or daily games where you get the thinking time back, or does something about the online format itself kill the patience regardless of the clock?
Our club does 90 minutes a side. It's a commitment but I enjoy it.

That's real classical chess — 90 minutes a side is a proper commitment, not a token gesture toward "slow chess." That's the kind of time control where you can actually calculate, sit with a position, second-guess yourself and come back around. Sounds like the club is giving you what online play can't, and the Thursday game is probably the one you actually look forward to rather than the one you grind through.

Are you keeping score / reviewing the games afterward, or is it more just play-and-move-on for now?
It suits me. I'd rather play one long game than six short ones.

That's a coherent preference, and it lines up with everything you've said — the frustration with online blitz, the appeal of 90 minutes a side, wanting time to actually think rather than pattern-match on reflex. Quality over volume, basically. One game where you're really *in* it beats six where you're just reacting.
Makes sense. Anyway, I have a game paused in front of me at the moment.
Nice — what's the position? Happy to look at it with you, whether that's "what should I be thinking about here" or you just want to talk through the plans out loud before you play your move.
